findings.title: Strategy shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool, breaking later strategy instances
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the pool is created by ResultsStrategyFactory and is shared across strategies. Arroyo may close a strategy during a rebalance and then create a new strategy from the same factory. Once close() has shut down the shared pool, worker threads are stopped and queues are closed, so the next strategy will submit to a dead pool. Its submit() exception handler can then mark offsets complete without processing. This can silently drop messages after any rebalance. The strategy should not shut down a factory-owned pool, or a new pool should be created per strategy.

findings.title: join() ignores its timeout and does not drain queued work before stopping commits
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join() simply calls close(), ignoring the timeout argument. close() stops the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains remaining queued items, and it never waits for queues or outstanding offsets to become empty. As a result, work processed during shutdown may never have its offsets committed, and shutdown can still block for fixed internal timeouts rather than respecting the requested join timeout.

findings.title: Shutdown flag can cause queued work items to be dropped
findings.body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before allowing queues to drain. OrderedQueueWorker.run() loops on while not self.shutdown, so if a worker is processing an item when shutdown begins it will exit after that one item even if its queue still contains pending work. Although q.shutdown(immediate=False) is intended to permit graceful draining, the worker flag prevents that and can discard queued messages without processing or committing them.

findings.title: Failed work items are marked complete and become eligible for commit
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches exceptions from the result processor and still calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows exceptions. Therefore a result that fails processing is treated as completed and can be committed, despite the strategy documentation saying offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient failure, such as a database or downstream outage, can permanently lose results with no retry or DLQ.

findings.title: OffsetTracker iterates shared partition dictionary while other threads may add partitions
findings.body: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets() iterates list(self.all_offsets.keys()) without a global lock, while add_offset() may concurrently create new partition entries in self.all_offsets from the submit thread. This can cause dictionary-changed-size-during-iteration errors or missed partitions in the commit loop. Per-partition locks protect individual offset sets but do not protect the partition key collection itself.

findings.title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite documented guarantee
findings.body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize and submit() puts work unconditionally. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll() only emits metrics and never applies backpressure. The class documentation claims natural backpressure when queues fill up, but unbounded queues never fill. If workers are slower than the consumer, messages and full Kafka payloads will accumulate in memory without bound and can OOM the process.

findings.title: FilteredPayload is handled through the generic exception path
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() passes FilteredPayload messages to the decoder. When used with ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload(), that decoder asserts the payload is not FilteredPayload, causing an AssertionError that is caught by the generic except branch and logged as 'Error submitting message to queue'. This turns normal filtered messages into exception log spam and relies on exception handling for control flow. FilteredPayload should be explicitly treated as a skipped/completed offset before decoding.

findings.title: Error-handling test is flaky and asserts behavior opposite to the implementation
findings.body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling mocks the result processor to raise for the first message and then asserts that no offsets were committed. However, the worker catches processing exceptions and marks the failed offset complete, so once the commit loop ticks the implementation will commit past the failed message. The test only waits briefly and may pass or fail depending on whether the 1-second commit loop runs before the assertion. It does not reliably validate the intended behavior and masks the fact that failed items are committed.
